A stairwell is the enclosed vertical shaft — essentially a tall, hollow column of space — built inside a building specifically to house a staircase. Think of it as the "room" that the stairs live inside.

When architects design a multi-storey building, they carve out a dedicated vertical channel from the ground floor all the way to the top. That channel has walls on all sides, a floor on each level, and an opening that lets you step onto each floor's corridor. The entire enclosed structure — the walls, the space within them, the landings, and the stairs themselves — is called the stairwell.

Imagine you are standing inside a tall building and you open a door marked "Staircase." You step into a separate, enclosed space — almost like a vertical tunnel or a box standing on its end. Above you, you can look up and see floor after floor of stairs going all the way to the top. Below you, if you look down, you can see the stairs descending to the ground. The sound of your footsteps echoes off the hard walls. That entire enclosed space you are standing in — from top to bottom — is the stairwell.

The key mental image: a stairwell is vertical. It cuts through the building like a shaft, and every floor has a door that opens into it.
How it differs from similar words

These words are related but not identical:

  • Stairs / steps — the individual horizontal surfaces you put your foot on to go up or down. Stairs are just the physical steps.
  • Staircase — the complete structure of steps, handrails, and banisters assembled together. A staircase is the thing you climb; it can exist in open spaces too (like a grand staircase in a luxury hotel lobby with no walls around it).
  • Stairway — similar to staircase; it refers to the path or passage formed by a set of stairs. It can be indoors or outdoors.
  • Stairwell — specifically the enclosed vertical space that contains and surrounds the staircase inside a building. The "well" part of the word signals that it is a deep, enclosed shaft — much like a water well is a deep, enclosed hole in the ground. Without enclosing walls, there is no stairwell — just a staircase.

So in simple terms: you climb a staircase, but you stand inside a stairwell.

Stairwells are found in virtually every multi-storey building:

  • Apartment buildings — usually near the lift or at each end of the corridor.
  • Office buildings — often placed near the corners of the building.
  • Schools, hospitals, shopping malls, hotels — anywhere people need to move between floors.
  • Residential homes with two or more floors — though in homes, the staircase is usually open (not walled off), so we rarely call it a stairwell in that context. The word "stairwell" is most naturally used for the enclosed, separate kind found in larger buildings.
Why stairwells are designed the way they are

Stairwells are not just practical for moving between floors — they serve a critical safety function. Because they are enclosed with walls and sealed with heavy, fire-resistant doors, they act as a protected escape route in case of fire or emergency. Smoke and flames have a much harder time entering a sealed stairwell, giving people a safer path to exit the building.

This is why you will often see signs saying "Use stairs in case of fire — do not use the lift." The stairwell, being enclosed and fireproofed, is the designated evacuation route.
Qualities and atmosphere of a stairwell

Stairwells have a distinctive character that makes them easy to recognise:

  • Echoes — because the space is enclosed by hard walls (often concrete or brick), sounds echo noticeably. Footsteps, voices, and even a dropped key will ring through a stairwell.
  • Slightly isolated feeling — stairwells are separate from the main corridors and rooms of a building. Closing the door behind you makes them feel removed from the activity of the rest of the building.
  • Vertical openness — looking up or down through the stairwell gives a sense of great height, because you can see all the floors stacked above and below.
  • Functional, not decorative — unlike the lobby or main corridors, stairwells are usually plain and utilitarian. They are there to work, not to impress.
How the word is used in sentences

• "During the fire drill, everyone gathered in the stairwell and waited for instructions."
  • "She could hear footsteps echoing in the stairwell before the door even opened."
  • "The building's stairwell runs from the basement all the way to the twelfth floor."
  • "He leaned over the railing inside the stairwell and looked down — the drop seemed enormous."
  • "The maintenance worker found a leak in the pipes running along the stairwell wall."
A stairwell is the enclosed vertical shaft built inside a multi-storey building that contains the staircase and provides a safe, walled passage between floors.
